dims.name: Recursion type
dims.q: What kind of recursion is it?

groups.name: Structural recursion
groups.desc: Follows the data definition: first/rest, left/right.

groups.name: Generative recursion
groups.desc: Subproblems are computed, not parts of the data.

groups.name: Linear recursion
groups.desc: One recursive call per step.

groups.name: Tree recursion
groups.desc: Two or more recursive calls per step.

groups.name: Recursive process
groups.desc: Work deferred and done on the way back.

groups.name: Iterative process
groups.desc: State carried down; nothing left to do on return.

dims.name: Decomposition
dims.q: How are the smaller instances laid out, and how many calls are drawn?

groups.name: Nested containment
groups.desc: Calls drawn inside their caller.

groups.name: Tree (node-link)
groups.desc: Calls linked to their subcalls.

groups.name: Linear chain
groups.desc: List of nodes and links.

groups.name: Stack
groups.desc: Frames piled up by depth.

groups.name: Table
groups.desc: Args, intermediates and results.

groups.name: Substitution trace
groups.desc: Expression rewritten until a value.

groups.name: Indentation staircase
groups.desc: Depth shown by indentation.

groups.name: Partition
groups.desc: Input split into boxed parts.

groups.name: Instance mapping
groups.desc: Size n aligned to size n−1.

groups.name: Metaphor / pictorial
groups.desc: Dolls, mirrors, spirals.

groups.name: Choice label
groups.desc: The decision named on the edge.

groups.name: Prune / fail + legend
groups.desc: Dead branches, keyed in a legend.

groups.name: Full expansion
groups.desc: Small input, every call drawn.

groups.name: Patterned elision
groups.desc: Rule implied by a few levels.

groups.name: Unpatterned elision
groups.desc: No inference can be made.

groups.name: Black-box leaf
groups.desc: Leaves drawn as opaque blocks.

groups.name: Deferred call
groups.desc: Subcall left unexpanded.

groups.name: Trusted subcall
groups.desc: The subcall’s result is used without drawing inside it (leap of faith).

dims.name: Self-referential data
dims.q: Which data refers to itself, and what sits inside one node?

groups.name: List
groups.desc: A list whose rest is again a list.

groups.name: Tree
groups.desc: A tree whose children are trees.

groups.name: Nested doll
groups.desc: A pictorial object holding a smaller copy.

groups.name: Concrete data
groups.desc: Values of the input itself.

groups.name: Call with arguments
groups.desc: The call as written, concrete args.

groups.name: State tuple
groups.desc: Only the changing parameters.

groups.name: Partial expression
groups.desc: Half-evaluated term, as in a trace.

dims.name: Return & combine
dims.q: How do results come back, and how many returns are drawn?

groups.name: Upward only
groups.desc: Results merging toward the root.

groups.name: Round trip
groups.desc: Down to the base case, then back up.

groups.name: Rewrite in place
groups.desc: Time runs down the lines.

groups.name: Return value
groups.desc: Value written on the way back.

groups.name: Combine step
groups.desc: How sub-results merge is drawn.

groups.name: Traversal path
groups.desc: Evaluation order traced.

groups.name: Call-step label
groups.desc: Each frame or step numbered.

groups.name: All returns drawn
groups.desc: Every call’s result is shown coming back.

groups.name: Some returns drawn
groups.desc: Only some results, e.g. the final one.

groups.name: Returns not drawn
groups.desc: Calls only; for a recursive process the way back is missing.

dims.name: Base case
dims.q: Is the stopping point shown, and how?

groups.name: Marked
groups.desc: Labelled or highlighted as the base case.

groups.name: Reached, not marked
groups.desc: The last call is drawn but not singled out.

groups.name: Dead-end leaf
groups.desc: A failed branch ends the recursion.

dims.name: Code Correspondence
dims.q: How does it tie back to the code?

groups.name: Diagram is code
groups.desc: Trace written in the program’s own syntax.

groups.name: Linked to the code
groups.desc: Placed next to it, arrowed into it, or sharing its names.

subs.name: Side by side
subs.desc: Diagram placed next to the code or rule.

subs.name: Arrows into code
subs.desc: Arrows tie parts of the diagram to code.

subs.name: Shared identifiers
subs.desc: Function and parameter names reused in nodes.

groups.name: Linked through math or prose
groups.desc: An equation or a written explanation, not the code.

subs.name: Recurrence only
subs.desc: Linked to an equation, not to code.

examples.title: Regular Expression Matching
examples.note: String states with (i, j) labels; dead branches crossed out.
examples.review: Branching on * and the (i, j) states are right; the true/false results are never shown coming back.

examples.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
examples.note: Six numbered steps push frames onto a stack, then return 12.
examples.review: Each frame’s arguments sit on a stack next to the code, and the final return 12 is shown; matches the recursive code.

examples.title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
examples.note: Links redrawn; the rest is said to be handled by the recursion.
examples.review: States plainly that links 3→4 must be fixed first by the recursive call, then relinks 1 and 2; correct order.

examples.title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
examples.note: The rest of the list bracketed and labelled “Recursive”.
examples.review: Only the two hand drawings show the recursive version; the other five images are input/output or the iterative pairwise swap.

examples.title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
examples.note: Before/after with the rest drawn as one “already done” box.
examples.review: Before/after with the rest drawn as an “already done” box: a clean leap-of-faith picture of the recursive step.

examples.title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
examples.note: curr/next links rewired over four frames.
examples.review: Shows the swap on a two-node list only; the recursive call on the rest never appears.

examples.title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
examples.note: Input, before swap, after swap and result rows.
examples.review: One local swap plus the final list; the recursion on the next pair is a single unexplained arrow.

examples.title: Reorder List
examples.note: Handwritten stack frames, each returning curr.
examples.review: Handwritten stack frames, each with its pointers and the value it returns; faithful to the recursive code.

examples.title: Remove Linked List Elements
examples.note: Return values written under arcs back along the list.
examples.review: Return values on the arcs (2, 2, NULL, NULL) are exactly what each call returns when removing 6.

examples.title: Reverse Linked List
examples.note: First/rest split; “reverse rest” trusted, then relinked.
examples.review: The first GIF animates the iterative while-loop; only the second (first / reverse rest / link rest) is the recursion.

examples.title: Reverse Linked List
examples.note: Three frames of node links being reversed.
examples.review: Relinking happens innermost-first, which is correct, but calls and returns are not shown.

examples.title: Reverse Linked List
examples.note: Columns of head, newHead and head-off per level.
examples.review: Columns of head, newHead and head-off per level show what each call returns while the list unwinds.

examples.title: Power of Two
examples.note: f(32) → f(16) → … → base case, return true back.
examples.review: f(32) → f(16) → … down to the base case, with true passed back up; values correct.

examples.title: Different Ways to Add Parentheses
examples.note: All expression trees for small inputs; G(3) = 5.
examples.review: Correct expression-tree counts (G(2) = 2, G(3) = 5), but it shows the answer space, not how the recursion builds it.

examples.title: Different Ways to Add Parentheses
examples.note: Five expression trees for 2*3-4*5 with their answers.
examples.review: All five trees for 2*3-4*5 and their values (−34, −10, −14, 10, −10) are right; the splitting recursion itself is not drawn.

examples.title: Different Ways to Add Parentheses
examples.note: Recursion trees with numbered return arrows, split cases I–III, memoisation.
examples.review: Split-by-operator recursion trees with the resulting values (−34, −14, −10) checked, plus where memoisation helps; one opening slide is a generic Fibonacci tree.

examples.title: Different Ways to Add Parentheses
examples.note: Each node annotated with its list of results.
examples.review: Every node carries its list of results, so the combine step is visible; values check out ([2] × [−17, −5] = [−34, −10]).

examples.title: Decode String
examples.note: a2[b2[cd]]e2[f] expanded level by level, results arrowed back.
examples.review: a2[b2[cd]]e2[f] expands level by level and the inner results are arrowed back into the outer string; correct.

examples.title: Predict the Winner
examples.note: P1/P2 levels over (i, j) states.
examples.review: Correct (i, j) states for each player, but the scores that come back are not shown.

examples.title: Fibonacci Number
examples.note: fib(5) call tree, every call drawn.
examples.review: Correct fib(5) call tree, calls only; it motivates the iterative solution the post actually uses.

examples.title: K-th Symbol in Grammar
examples.note: Whiteboard hypothesis → induction → base condition → code.
examples.review: Correct hypothesis → induction → base-case reasoning, but the whiteboard is crowded and hard to follow.

examples.title: K-th Symbol in Grammar
examples.note: The grammar rows drawn as a tree.
examples.review: Draws the whole grammar tree; the recursion only walks one root-to-leaf path, which the picture does not distinguish.

examples.title: All Possible Full Binary Trees
examples.note: Pick a root, box left and right groups, combine subtrees.
examples.review: Partition and subtree combination are right, but nodes are numbered 1–7 like a BST although full-binary-tree nodes carry no values.

examples.title: All Possible Full Binary Trees
examples.note: All five tree shapes for F(7).
examples.review: All five shapes of F(7) are correct; it shows results, not the recursion.

examples.title: Find Kth Bit in Nth Binary String
examples.note: (k, n, mid) reduced step by step; “normal world / mirror world”.
examples.review: A careful step-by-step trace of (k, n, mid), including a deliberately wrong answer that is then corrected with the mirror idea.

examples.title: Find the Winner of the Circular Game
examples.note: j(n−1, k, i) mapped onto j(n, k, i+1).
examples.review: The j(n−1, k, i) / j(n, k, i+1) notation is not explained, so the mapping is hard to verify from the picture.

examples.title: Find the Winner of the Circular Game
examples.note: Circle, elimination, then n = 7 renumbered onto n = 6 (+4).
examples.review: Renumbering n = 7 onto n = 6 with +4 (mod 7) is exactly the step the recursion undoes on return; values correct.

examples.title: Find the Winner of the Circular Game
examples.note: Circles relabelled, then f(n, k) = (f(n−1, k) + k − 1) % n + 1.
examples.review: Circles relabelled, then f(n, k) = (f(n−1, k) + k − 1) % n + 1 with f(1, k) = 1; correct.

examples.title: Different Ways to Add Parentheses
examples.note: Expression trees (same figure as solution 1294189).
examples.review: Reuses the same expression-tree figure as solution 1294189; correct, but not this author’s own diagram.
